newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Bosnian Serbs silent over "cleansing" legacy.
newsitem.headline: Bosnian Serbs silent over "cleansing" legacy.

text.p: Stony silence grips ethnic Serbs living near former detention camps in northwestern Bosnia when an international war crimes trial in the Netherlands is discussed.

As the International Criminal Tribunal for former Yugoslavia prepares to deliver a verdict on Wednesday in the case of Dusan Tadic, most Serbs in the Prijedor region deny the premise of the trial itself.
Tadic, a Bosnian Serb, is accused of committing atrocities against Moslem inmates during the brutal "ethnic cleansing" campaign conducted by Serb authorities at the beginning of the 1992-95 war.

Survivors have told the tribunal of murder, torture and hunger at detention camps in northwest Bosnia. Expert witnesses have described systematic deportations of Moslems and Croats as part of a policy to carve out a separate Serb state.
But Serbs in the Prijedor region, where three notorious detention camps existed, prefer not to speak of the camps and deny any atrocities took place.

"In Prijedor and everywhere in former Yugoslavia, the Serbs were only defending themselves," said a pensioner in a local cafe. "There were Moslem terrorists who had weapons and were planning to attack."
The pensioner said Serb forces were forced to take pre-emptive action, mindful of the World War Two-era slaughter of Serbs in the region.
"At least here we didn't allow a Croat to take out 20 Serbs into the forest and slit their throats," the pensioner's friend said.
The ruling Serb Democratic Party has steadfastly denied any crimes were committed around Prijedor and police have intimidated and even beaten those who have spoken to human rights investigators.
In a ceremony last week , Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic awarded medals to 37 Serb police for their role in the "liberation" of Prijedor in 1992.
Three suspects indicted in connection with the detention camps now work as policemen in the Prijedor area despite demands for them to step down, U.N. officials say.

The same men who orchestrated the expulsions of non-Serbs and the seizure of property through a wartime "crisis committee" still run Prijedor and surrounding towns, a recent Human Rights Watch report said.
The U.S.-based organisation reported that members of the circle include Milomir Stakic, who became mayor of Prijedor after the elected mayor, a Moslem, was detained and never seen again.

Peacetime has proved profitable for the ethnic cleansers. Public companies all controlled by the former crisis committee have received tens of thousands of dollars in international reconstruction aid, Human Rights Watch reported.
Political commentators warn that failure to prosecute ethnic cleansers could ultimately feed the flames of another war in the Balkans.
A few Bosnian Serb opposition activists and independent journalists have condemned the expulsions that occurred five years ago and say war crimes trials should establish who was responsible.

Serbs in Prijedor need to shrug off their "collective amnesia", journalist Radmila Karlas wrote last month. "Because only by naming those responsible will it be possible to rid themselves of the burden."
